Meeting dates The committee met on the follow dates: Tuesday 11/15 Weds 1/25 Weds 2/22 Thurs 3/30 Weds 4/26 Executive Summary: The JCODL, which reconvened in 2022-2023 after a pandemic-related hiatus, considered two key priorities during the current academic year: ● Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses ● URI Instructional Modalities and Descriptions The Committee is recommending Faculty Senate action on these two items, including rescission of the 2013 “Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses”, and adoption of revised definitions of instructional modalities which clarify course delivery for faculty and students. Committee Recommendations 1. Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses.

Context: In 2013, an “ Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses ” was approved by the Faculty Senate, though never included in the manual or any other official venue, concerning exams for online courses.
In short, this policy allowed for online courses to require in-person proctored exams, whether on one of the URI campuses, or at an approved venue elsewhere.
Should the student be unable to travel to a URI campus, it was the student’s responsibility to find an appropriate venue and an approved proctor, AND to shoulder any related fees.
This policy was brought to light in 2022 by a faculty member teaching an online undergraduate course who wished to require a proctored in-person exam on the Kingston campus.
Discussion: The committee discussed this policy and its ramifications at some length, including the fact that it was not in the University Manual, etc.

Discussion further circulated around the fact that best practices for online instruction recommend against proctored exams due to issues with proctoring services such as lockdown browsers, questions of access and fairness to all learners, privacy concerns, the fact that a key reason that learners enroll in online classes relates to scheduling flexibility, and that most courses can be effectively assessed without the use of high-stakes, in-person exams.
Recommendation: It is the recommendation of the Joint Committee for Online/Distance Learning that the Faculty Senate rescind the 2013 “Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses”.
Courses delivered in a fully online modality should assess students through the online modality.
Fully online certificate/degree programs with accreditation requirements related to assessment may implement remote proctoring solutions at no additional cost to students.
The Office of ATL is available to support faculty as they develop assessments for their online courses. 2.
Definitions of learning modalities.

Context: Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face < 25% online, Blended 25-75% online, Online 75-100% online), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.
The work: The committee spent a large amount of time researching, discussing, evaluating, and compiling a list of instructional modalities in the digital space.
Recommendation: The committee recommends that the Faculty Senate and University adopt, institutionalize, and publicize the following learning modality definitions and descriptions.
The committee further recommends that the Faculty Senate review the approval process for blended and online courses, including the percentage ranges of online delivery.

URI Instructional Modalities and Descriptions The following recommendations are the result of collaborative effort by the JCDOL membership which includes representation of faculty across the Colleges, URI’s Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning, ITS Teaching and Learning, and the Office of the Provost, and.
Past and current practice at URI, best-practices in online education, and a review of online education definitions in use at peer-institutions were used to develop the following overview of the

university’s instructional modalities, a definition of each, and considerations for implementation starting in the Fall 2023 semester. Definitions Modality (location/ meeting arrangement) Description In-person All instruction occurs in a specified physical location and on specified days/times. Blended* I nstruction combines both in person meetings on speciﬁed days/times and online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus on the ﬁrst day of class. Online synchronous* All instruction occurs online at specified days/times. Online mixed* All i nstruction occurs online in a combination of synchronous meetings on speciﬁed days/times and asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and the weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction are clear to students in the syllabus. Online asynchronous All instruction occurs online with no specified meeting days/times. The weekly time commitment to online asynchronous instruction is clear to students in the syllabus. Considerations for Implementation Schedule : Regardless of modality, the schedule of all required meetings must be made clear in the syllabus and in eCampus to ensure that students understand the pattern of required meetings. Time Commitment : The approximate weekly time commitment (time on task) for asynchronous instructional activities should be clear in the syllabus so that students can plan their schedules for greatest success. Per 8.31.10 Basis for Credit, “ the student workload for an online class shall be equivalent to the in-class and out-of-class work in its face-to-face equivalent.” For

example, “ For this 3-credit hour in-person semester course, you should expect to spend around three hours in class each week and an average of six hours preparing for class (this includes readings, homework, and other assigned activities),” and for an online class “For this 3-credit hour online class you should expect to spend three hours per week completing online instructional activities, and an additional six hours on related activities, including readings, homework, online discussions, and other assigned activities.” Synchronous Online and Online Mixed Modality options : Asynchronous online delivery of courses and degree programs is designed to increase student access to education by reducing the barriers to attendance presented by conflicts between work-life responsibilities and scheduled in-person classes. This student access lens should therefore be centered in decisions and policies about the use and scheduling of synchronous and mixed online courses. The scheduling of synchronous online classes during standard working/class hours (e.g. M-F 8-5) creates barriers to attendance and should be avoided. We recommend, however, that flexibility be extended to J-Term, summer, evening, and graduate program classes, particularly for the modalities noted above with an asterisk (*). Chris Lavan, Associate Vice Provost, ATL, JCODL Chair Purpose of the Committee The purpose of the Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning (JCODL) is to propose, examine, and recommend institutional policies and practices for developing, planning, and evaluating online and distance learning with a focus on quality, sustainability, and connection to the University’s mission, with approval of the Faculty Senate and Provost.
Further, JCODL, considers faculty training, quality in delivery of online offerings, student learning outcomes, and ADA compliance regarding online and distance learning, as well as develops and implements strategic plans for online courses, certificate, and degree programs. (University Manual 5.78.10 - 5.78.11).
Executive Summary The committee discussed several topics internally (listed in the next section) during the 2024-2025 academic year, and brought forth one proposal for consideration and a vote to the university’s Faculty Senate.

Proposal: Updated Adoption of New Course Modalities and Methods of Instruction This proposal had been a priority of this committee for three academic years, and with collaboration between several Faculty Senators, including past Curriculum and Standards 1

Committee (CASC) Chair and Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) member Senator Preisser, as well as the Office of the Provost and University Registrar’s Office, the proposal was introduced during the November 2024 Faculty Senate meeting.
At the November Faculty Senate meeting the proposal was tabled, but then brought back to the floor of the Faculty Senate during its January 2025 meeting where it was approved by a vote during that same meeting.
Ultimately, the initial proposal for updated recognized teaching methods evolved to include methods of instruction as well.

A portion of the slides presented during that January 2025 meeting are included within this report under section “Appendix A: Sample presentation slides of proposed course modalities and methods of instruction”, and the official titles of each proposal are listed directly below. ● FSEC Report #2024-2025-02 - Proposal to define the various modalities of instruction within the University Manual ● FSEC Report #2025-2025-03 - Proposal to define the various methods of instruction within the University Manual Internal Topics of Discussion During the 2024-25 Academic Year ● Reviewed Data Related to 2023-2024 Participation and Completion Rates of URI Instructors Engaging the 4 Qualification Pathways to Teach Online at URI ○ Outcome: ■ 83 new faculty qualified to teach online during the 2023-2024 academic year. ● Reviewed New Self-Paced Option for Online Pedagogy Experience ○ Outcomes: ■ Piloted over Summer 2024 and softly launched for the 2024-2025 academic year. ■ Completed by 13 instructors with generally positive feedback from participants. ● Reviewed Online Teaching Recommendation Qualification Survey ○ Outcome ■ This new tool was presented to the committee during the 2024-25 academic year.

It’s a resource intended to provide guidance to URI instructors about which of the 4 pathways for qualifying to teach online would be best suited for them based on their level of experience teaching online. ■ Feedback from the committee was received and used to improve this tool. 2

■ It was launched during the spring 2025 semester. ● JCODL hosted presentations from: ○ Beth Mendenhall, Associate Professor, Marine Affairs ■ Topic: Discussion on auditing online courses and online learning policy transparency ○ Jen Riley, Dean, College of Arts & Sciences ■ Topic: Discussion on approval process for courses already approved to be taught in-person but that also could be taught online ○ Michelle Rogers, JCODL Member and Director, Teaching & Learning Services ■ Topic: Brightspace Change Management Report ○ Outcomes: ■ Information was received and discussed by JCODL committee members. ■ No changes were made to URI Online or ATL operations. ■ No recommendations were developed upon the completion of the presentations or the committee’s discussions. ● Drafted a Plan for Implementing the Course Modalities and Methods of Instruction ○ Outcomes: ■ A plan was discussed amongst a subset of the committee during the spring 2025 semester. ■ Chris Lavan, chair of the JCODL, contacted Jack Humphrey of the University's Registrar’s Office about formulating a plan for collaborative support to academic departments during the summer of 2025. ■ The Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning hosted a Summer Institute on Blended Teaching from May - June 2025 , and the new course modalities and methods of instruction were introduced to participants. ■ Since then a webpage resource defining each updated teaching method and method of instruction has been created and disseminated to Deans, Assistant and Associate Deans, Department Chairs, and other campus groups beginning in August 2025. ● A link to that new webpage resource is here: Course Modalities & Teaching Methods – Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning ● Reviewed Data Related to 2024-2025 Participation and Completion Rates of URI Instructors Engaging the 4 Qualification Pathways to Teach Online at URI ○ Outcomes: ■ 84 new faculty qualified to teach online during the 2024-2025 academic year. 3
